reasoning: The paper uses established, existing research software tools (Freesurfer, PMOD, SPM12, MATLAB curve fitting toolbox, IBM SPSS) for processing and statistical analysis, with no claim of creating or significantly extending any software (S2). The researchers collected new PET imaging (11C-PBR28, 18F-flortaucipir), MRI, neuropsychological, and neuropathological data from recruited patients and controls specifically for this study, constituting newly generated research data (D1), even though the data availability statement indicates it is only available upon request.

The paper generates substantial new research data: 3147 spectroscopic host-galaxy redshifts newly measured for PS1 transients, a newly curated photometric SN sample with cuts, and large SNANA Monte Carlo simulation outputs tailored to PS1 (D1). It also creates new research software: the authors implement their own BEAMS analysis code (combining an MCMC sampler via emcee with a custom likelihood and CosmoMC interface) specifically for this study, stating "Our code is available online" with a GitHub link (djones1040/BEAMS) and example input files — this is a created computational workflow/implementation, not just use of a generic tool. While the paper also uses existing software (SNANA, SALT2, PSNID, emcee, CosmoMC, SExtractor, RVSAO), the clear claim of having built their own BEAMS implementation elevates it to S1, and per the general rule, generated supersedes used.

The paper uses existing software (R, and the research packages "mgcv" and "jtrans") for statistical modeling but does not create or extend any software itself, so it is S2. For data, although much of the phenotypic/immunological time-series data derives from a previous experiment, the paper newly genotyped 34 animals for PTPRC alleles using an RFLP assay and capillary electrophoresis, generating new research data (genotype calls) that did not exist before and are central to this study's novel analysis. Since generating data implies also using it, and new genotype data was created, this is classified as D1 (data generated).

This is a conceptual/theoretical literature review paper that analyzes whether the Balanced Scorecard embodies bureaucratic principles. It explicitly states "This paper does not offer empirical support for the arguments made" - it relies solely on literature review and conceptual mapping (Table 2), with no research software created or used, and no research data (datasets, surveys, interviews, etc.) collected or analyzed.

This is a literature review paper that surveys and synthesizes existing research on energy storage for water desalination systems powered by renewable energy. It does not report any software created or used by the authors (all simulations/models mentioned are from cited third-party studies), nor does it generate or use any research data of its own—it only summarizes findings, figures, and tables from other publications. Hence it falls into S3D3: No Research Software, No Research Data.

The paper uses existing machine learning software tools (Weka, JADBio, and the SANN technique from prior work) to analyze data rather than developing new research software, so it qualifies as S2 (software used). Regarding data, while the 192-patient AQ/EQ/RQ dataset was reused from a prior paper, the authors also designed two novel screening questionnaires (ASTA tools) and administered them to new cohorts of 30 and 18 patients, collecting new survey/assessment data analyzed statistically in the paper. This constitutes generation of new research data, so D1 applies (generation takes precedence over use per the general rules).

The paper's core contribution is a novel hierarchical energy management system implemented as software: a MILP optimization, ANFIS forecasting, adaptive autoregression forecasting, and a real-time predictive controller, coded as embedded MATLAB functions within a LabVIEW control platform specifically developed for this research (not just generic tools used as a utility, but the implemented control algorithm itself is the contribution) — this qualifies as Research Software Generated (S1). The authors also built and ran a laboratory microgrid testbed at the University of Nottingham, producing new experimental measurement data (actual/reference power drawn, BESS SOC, load/PV profiles, timing measurements) generated through this fieldwork, which qualifies as Research Data Generated (D1), even though some earlier simulation inputs (CREST-modelled load profiles, SODA weather data, PVOutput.org PV data) were pre-existing used data.

The paper generates new research data: raw multi-track Ambisonic recordings and 360° videos collected in Peace Gardens, Sheffield, and experimental survey/questionnaire data (SQE and LoW responses from 120 participants), deposited openly on Mendeley Data (D1). No research software is created or claimed as a contribution; tools used (Adobe Audition for editing, SPSS and Matlab) are generic/utility software for processing/statistical analysis, not research software developed or significantly extended by the authors (S3).

The paper collected new original behavioral observation data (CCTV footage of binturong activity/behavior) during zoo open/closed conditions, which constitutes newly generated research data (D1). For analysis, the authors only used R for statistical tests and Microsoft Excel for data entry—both are generic statistical/data processing tools explicitly excluded from the research software definition, and no custom research software was created or claimed as a contribution, so this is S3 (No Research Software).

This paper reports a post-hoc analysis of the SSaSS cluster-randomised trial, generating new clinical/cancer outcome data (fatal and non-fatal cancer events identified via follow-up, record linkage, and adjudication) specifically for this analysis, which qualifies as research data generated (D1). No research software was created or claimed as a contribution; statistical analyses were performed with SAS, a generic statistical package used only as a utility tool, which falls under S3 (No Research Software).

The study collects new EEG-fMRI, structural MRI, and clinical/surgical outcome data from 10 epilepsy patients specifically for this research, constituting generated research data (D1). For analysis, the authors use existing, established neuroimaging software tools (SPM12/DCM10, FSL, FreeSurfer, 3D Slicer/Freeview, SEEGA, ICN_Atlas) without claiming to create or significantly extend any new software — they apply standard DCM methodology to a new clinical dataset, so this is Software Used (S2) rather than generated.

This is a narrative review article summarizing and synthesizing findings from previously published GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on type 2 diabetes and cancer genetics. It does not report creating or using any research software (no tools, pipelines, or code are described as part of this paper's own methodology), nor does it generate or use any specific research dataset—it discusses results/conclusions from other studies' literature, which falls under "Literature and Papers" rather than research data itself. No data generation or usage, and no software generation or usage is claimed.

The paper develops a conceptual "agile smart lean-green" model and validates it through two real-world case studies (automobile and mining machinery shop floors), collecting observational/measurement data via Gemba walks, interviews, and brainstorming sessions (production times, uptime, downtime, ergonomics issues, etc., in Tables 2-5). This constitutes newly generated research data (fieldwork observations), confirmed by the Data Availability Statement noting data are available on request. No research software is created or used as a contribution—"design software" is only mentioned as a suggested future action, never actually implemented or used in the study—so this is S3 for software.

The paper is an empirical economics study analyzing existing panel survey data from the Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS, 2002-2019) to study adaptation to vulnerability. It uses pre-existing survey data (not collected or generated by the authors) to derive statistics and regression findings, which fits D2 (Research Data Used). There is no mention of any research software created or significantly extended by the authors—only standard econometric estimation (fixed-effects regressions, ordered logit) presumably run with generic statistical software, which does not count as research software under the criteria, placing it in S3 (No Research Software).

The paper is a purely theoretical/mathematical work on matrix decomposition theorems and proofs, with no mention of creating or using research software (no code, packages, or implementations described), and explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article." The Wilson matrix example is a mathematical illustration, not research data.

The paper uses an existing numerical convection model/code (described in Willis et al. 2007, "available on request from the corresponding author") rather than claiming to create or significantly extend new software, so software is Used (S2) not Generated. The authors ran a new suite of rotating convection simulations (68 simulations, including six new ones with hemispheric CMB heat flux forcing) producing new simulation output data (temperature/velocity fields, etc.), which constitutes generated research data (D1), as noted in the Data availability statement referring to "the findings of this study."

The paper analyzes publicly available long-read sequencing data from the NABEC cohort (existing dataset, not newly generated by this study), making it Data Used (D2); the novel insertions/SVs reported are findings derived from this existing data, not newly generated research data. The study relies entirely on existing software/pipelines (Napu, Sniffles2, EMBOSS/Transeq, FASTA, RepeatMasker, BLAST, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram, Plotrix, tidyverse, FigTree) with no claim of creating or significantly extending any software, so it is Software Used (S2).

The paper uses existing surveillance/traveler case data (WHO reports, laboratory-confirmed MERS cases, travel statistics) to derive cumulative incidence estimates via a mathematical formula/method adapted from prior work (Cauchemez et al.). This is use of existing research data (findings/statistics derived from a data source = D2), not generation of new data. No research software (e.g., named tool, script, or model implementation) is claimed as created or used as a contribution; the calculations appear to be a straightforward formula application, classifying as S3.

The paper reports original fieldwork/laboratory findings: shark specimens collected, copepods dissected, and histological sections prepared and examined, generating new observational/image data (Figs. 1-2) specific to this study. No research software (generated or used) is mentioned anywhere—only generic lab equipment (autostainer) and museum deposition of physical specimens, which is not software. Hence S3 (no software) and D1 (data generated).

The study isolated 44 new flavobacterial phages, sequenced their genomes, generated metagenomic datasets, 16S rRNA sequences, and TEM/FISH measurements — all newly generated research data (D1). For analysis, the authors used numerous existing third-party software tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, GRAViTy, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLASTN, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, ARB, RAxML, MiGA, Geneious) without claiming to have created or substantially extended any of them, so this is software used rather than generated (S2).

The paper conducts an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study, generating synthetic data under various model misspecification scenarios (local dependence, nonnormal latent distributions) — this counts as research data generated (D1). It also applies the tests to an existing real dataset (Miller et al., 1984), but since data was generated, D1 takes precedence per the general rule. On software, the authors use R's built-in 'optim' function and the 'NumDeriv' package for numerical derivatives; these are generic statistical/computational utility tools used for processing, not research software created, significantly extended, or claimed as a contribution by the authors, so this is S3.

The paper describes the creation of the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, an online software tool built (under contract by Anthesis group) specifically for this research, with authors credited for "Software" contributions in the CRediT statement — this constitutes software generated (S1). The paper also reports newly generated research data: the expert elicitation/evidence-assessment scores for hundreds of actions across species groups and biomes, compiled via a structured Delphi-style process and provided as Supplementary Table S12, representing data created/generated by the research (D1). While some existing data (Conservation Evidence database entries, an example farm's data from Bidwells) is used as input, the general rule that generated status takes precedence applies, placing this in S1D1.

The paper reports original experimental work (solid dispersion preparation and characterization via PXRD, DSC, FTIR, and dissolution studies), generating new research data (diffractograms, thermograms, spectra, dissolution profiles). No research software was created or used as a contribution—only generic instrument/analysis software (EVA, TA Universal Analysis, OMNIC) was used as a utility for data processing, which counts as S3 per the criteria.

This is an archival/historical analysis of exhibition design in interwar Britain, drawing on letters, catalogues, and secondary literature. It does not claim to use or create any research software. The archival materials (letters, exhibition catalogues) function as primary historical sources/literature for a qualitative historical argument, not as research data generated or used per the UKRI definition (and literature/documents are explicitly excluded as research data). No datasets, measurements, or structured research data are created or analyzed.

This is a scoping review that extracts and synthesizes data/findings from seven existing clinical studies (D2: data used, not generated). The tools mentioned (Excel worksheet, EndNote) are generic data management/reference software used as utilities, not research software created or significantly extended by the authors, so S3 applies.

The paper reports a newly synthesized compound and its single-crystal X-ray diffraction structure determination, generating new research data (cell parameters, atomic coordinates, bond lengths/angles, hydrogen-bond geometry, displacement parameters). This counts as generated research data. For software, the authors used established third-party crystallographic programs (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND, SHELXTL) for data collection, structure solution/refinement, and visualization, with no claim of having created or extended any software themselves — so this is Software Used (S2), not Generated.

The study generated new research data through interviews and focus group discussions (22 teachers), which were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed - this constitutes generated research data (D1). The paper mentions using NVivo for coding, but this is a generic qualitative data analysis utility used only for processing/organizing data, not a research software contribution in its own right, and no other research software was created or used as a research contribution, so this falls under S3.

This is a narrative literature review synthesizing published studies on protein-ionic liquid interactions (keratins, collagens, silks, plant proteins, enzymes). The authors did not create or use any research software themselves—mentions of simulations, COSMO-RS, or MD are all references to other researchers' prior work, not tools employed in this paper. Similarly, the tables (e.g., solubility values) are summaries of findings from the cited literature rather than research data collected, generated, or analyzed by the authors; per the criteria, literature/papers are explicitly excluded from research data. No evidence of software or data generation/use by this paper itself, so it falls under S3D3.

This is a qualitative, longitudinal single-case study (Ach. Brito) in brand management research. The authors collected primary research data through 25 personal interviews, non-participant observations, and document/archival research over 2007-2014, which constitutes generated research data (D1). There is no mention of any research software being created or used (e.g., no specialized tools, models, or code) — only interpretive qualitative analysis is described, so this is S3.

This is an experimental physics paper reporting room-temperature ODMR measurements on single hBN defects. The authors generated substantial original research data: PL spectra, second-order intensity-correlation (g2(τ)) measurements, ODMR spectra as functions of magnetic field/angle, and fit parameters — all newly collected via their confocal/ODMR setup (D1). The "Code availability" statement refers only to custom analysis scripts (fitting routines for g2 decays, Lorentzian fits) used as a utility to process and fit their data; the paper does not claim to have created or significantly extended research software as a contribution in its own right, so per the criteria this falls under S3 (no research software).
